---
title: "Relationships and flows"
description: "Scatter plots, hexbins, heatmaps, chords, Sankey diagrams and networks."
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(ddplot)
library(ggplot2) # mpg, diamonds
library(dplyr)
```

Charts for the relationship between two numeric variables, for two-way tables, and for flows and networks between categories.

::: {.dd-chooser}

| Chart | Use it when |
|---|---|
| [`scatter_plot()`](#scatter_plot) | You look at the relationship between two numeric variables, optionally by group, with bubbles or a trend line |
| [`hexbin_plot()`](#hexbin_plot) | A scatter plot has too many points to read |
| [`chord_diagram()`](#chord_diagram) | You show flows between categories, such as migration or trade |
| [`heatmap_chart()`](#heatmap_chart) | You show a value for every pair of two categories, such as a correlation matrix |
| [`sankey_diagram()`](#sankey_diagram) | You show how quantities flow and split through the stages of a process |
| [`network_graph()`](#network_graph) | You show who is connected to whom, and the clusters that emerge |

:::

## `scatter_plot()` {#scatter_plot}

A scatter plot shows how two numeric variables move together. Hover a point to read its values; drag a box to select points, then use **Zoom** to look closer (double-click resets the view).

```{r}
scatter_plot(
  data = mpg,
  x = "displ",
  y = "hwy",
  x_title = "Engine displacement (litres)",
  y_title = "Highway miles per gallon",
  title = "Bigger engines, fewer miles"
)
```

### Groups and trend lines

`group` colours the points by a column. The legend is interactive: click an entry to hide a group, double-click to keep only that group. `trend = "lm"` fits a linear regression per group, with its 95% confidence band; hover a line to read its slope, intercept and R².

```{r}
scatter_plot(
  data = iris,
  x = "Sepal.Length",
  y = "Petal.Length",
  group = "Species",
  trend = "lm",
  title = "Petal and sepal length by species"
)
```

### Bubbles, colour scales and labels

`size_by` maps a third variable to the point area. A numeric `group` gives a colour gradient. `label` names each point in the tooltip, and `show_labels` writes some of them on the chart (labels that would overlap are skipped). `tooltip` adds more columns to the tooltip, and `trend = "loess"` draws a smooth curve.

```{r}
cars <- mtcars
cars$model <- rownames(mtcars)

scatter_plot(
  data = cars,
  x = "hp",
  y = "mpg",
  size_by = "disp",
  group = "qsec",
  label = "model",
  show_labels = c("Maserati Bora", "Toyota Corolla", "Lotus Europa", "Cadillac Fleetwood"),
  tooltip = c("cyl", "gear"),
  trend = "loess",
  title = "Horsepower and fuel economy",
  subtitle = "Bubble area: displacement. Colour: quarter-mile time (s)"
)
```

### Log scales and reference lines

Skewed variables are easier to read on a log scale (`x_scale`, `y_scale`). `h_lines` and `v_lines` draw labelled reference lines.

```{r}
states <- data.frame(
  state      = rownames(state.x77),
  region     = state.region,
  area       = state.x77[, "Area"],
  population = state.x77[, "Population"],
  income     = state.x77[, "Income"]
)

scatter_plot(
  data = states,
  x = "area",
  y = "population",
  group = "region",
  label = "state",
  show_labels = TRUE,
  tooltip = "income",
  x_scale = "log",
  y_scale = "log",
  h_lines = c("Median population" = median(states$population)),
  x_title = "Area (square miles)",
  y_title = "Population (thousands, 1975)",
  title = "US states: area and population"
)
```

### In Shiny

Inside a Shiny app, the chart reports what the user selects. With `d3Output("cars")`, `input$cars_selected` holds the row numbers of `data` inside the brushed box, and `input$cars_clicked` the row of the last clicked point:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
output$cars <- renderD3(scatter_plot(mtcars, "wt", "mpg"))
output$picked <- renderTable(mtcars[input$cars_selected, ])
```

## `hexbin_plot()` {#hexbin_plot}

`hexbin_plot()` is inspired by the hexbin transform of [Observable Plot](https://observablehq.com/plot/transforms/hexbin). It groups points into a grid of hexagons coloured by the number of observations in each one, which keeps dense scatter plots readable. The binning is written by hand, since d3-hexbin is not bundled with r2d3.

```{r}
hexbin_plot(
  data     = faithful,
  x        = "waiting",
  y        = "eruptions",
  bin_width = 14,
  x_title   = "Waiting time to next eruption (min)",
  y_title   = "Eruption duration (min)",
  title    = "Old Faithful eruptions"
)
```

A log colour scale helps when counts are very skewed:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
dsample <- diamonds[sample(nrow(diamonds), 10000), ]

hexbin_plot(
  data         = dsample,
  x            = "carat",
  y            = "price",
  bin_width     = 8,
  color_palette = "Viridis",
  color_scale   = "log",
  title        = "Diamond price by carat"
)
```

## `chord_diagram()` {#chord_diagram}

`chord_diagram()` shows the flows between a set of entities as outer arcs joined by ribbons. Its look and hover behaviour are inspired by the chord chart of [Nivo](https://nivo.rocks/chord/): hovering over an entity fades every ribbon not connected to it, and clicking an arc pins the highlight.

```{r}
migration <- data.frame(
  from  = c("Africa", "Africa", "Africa", "Asia", "Asia", "Asia",
            "Europe", "Europe", "Latin America", "Latin America",
            "North America", "Oceania", "Asia", "Europe"),
  to    = c("Europe", "North America", "Asia", "Europe", "North America",
            "Oceania", "North America", "Asia", "North America", "Europe",
            "Europe", "Asia", "Africa", "Oceania"),
  value = c(420, 150, 90, 610, 520, 230, 180, 120, 870, 260,
            95, 40, 60, 75)
)

chord_diagram(
  data        = migration,
  from        = "from",
  to          = "to",
  value       = "value",
  value_format = ",.0f",
  title       = "Migration flows between regions (illustrative data)"
)
```

A square matrix with dimnames works too:

```{r}
hair <- matrix(
  c(11975,  5871, 8916, 2868,
     1951, 10048, 2060, 6171,
     8010, 16145, 8090, 8045,
     1013,   990,  940, 6907),
  nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE,
  dimnames = list(c("Black", "Blond", "Brown", "Red"),
                  c("Black", "Blond", "Brown", "Red"))
)

chord_diagram(
  data        = hair,
  colors      = c("#3b3b3b", "#f2c45a", "#8c5a3c", "#d0533a"),
  ribbon_color = "gradient",
  pad_angle    = 0.05,
  value_format = ",.0f",
  title       = "Hair color flows"
)
```

## `heatmap_chart()` {#heatmap_chart}

A heatmap colours a grid of cells, one per pair of two categorical columns. With a `value` column, the rows of each pair are aggregated (`aggregate`); without one, the cells count the rows. Hover a cell to read its value and see it on the colour legend.

```{r}
aq <- airquality
aq$Month <- factor(month.abb[aq$Month], levels = month.abb[5:9])
aq$Week <- paste("Week", (aq$Day - 1) %/% 7 + 1)
heatmap_chart(aq, x = "Month", y = "Week", value = "Temp", aggregate = "mean",
              colors = c("#fff3d6", "#ffb15c", "#d6402b"), value_format = ".0f",
              title = "Temperature in New York (F)")
```

With a `midpoint`, the colours diverge around it, which suits correlations and changes. `cluster = TRUE` reorders the rows and the columns so that similar ones sit together:

```{r}
cors <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor(mtcars)))
names(cors) <- c("var1", "var2", "correlation")
heatmap_chart(cors, x = "var1", y = "var2", value = "correlation",
              midpoint = 0, cluster = TRUE, title = "Correlations in mtcars")
```

## `sankey_diagram()` {#sankey_diagram}

A Sankey diagram shows flows as bands whose width is proportional to their value. Each row of the data is a flow from a `source` to a `target`; the nodes are placed in columns from left to right. Hover a flow or a node to highlight it, and drag a node up or down to untangle the diagram.

```{r}
budget <- data.frame(
  from = c("Salary", "Salary", "Freelance", "Freelance", "Savings",
           "Savings", "Living", "Living", "Living"),
  to = c("Living", "Savings", "Living", "Savings", "Stocks",
         "Emergency fund", "Rent", "Food", "Transport"),
  amount = c(2600, 900, 500, 300, 700, 500, 1700, 900, 500)
)
sankey_diagram(budget, source = "from", target = "to", value = "amount",
               value_format = "$,.0f", title = "Where the money goes")
```

Several steps can be chained by stacking the flows of each step. Here, who survived the Titanic, by class and sex, with flows coloured from their source to their target:

```{r}
tt <- as.data.frame(Titanic)
tt$Survived <- ifelse(tt$Survived == "Yes", "Survived", "Died")
step1 <- aggregate(Freq ~ Class + Sex, data = tt, FUN = sum)
step2 <- aggregate(Freq ~ Sex + Survived, data = tt, FUN = sum)
names(step1) <- names(step2) <- c("from", "to", "people")
sankey_diagram(rbind(step1, step2), source = "from", target = "to",
               value = "people", link_color = "gradient",
               colors = c(Died = "#9498a0", Survived = "#3ca951"))
```

## `network_graph()` {#network_graph}

A network graph places connected nodes close to each other with a force simulation, so that clusters appear on their own. Give the links as a data frame (`from`, `to`, optionally a `weight`) and, optionally, the nodes as a second data frame to colour them by group, size them or label them. Hover a node to highlight its neighbours, drag it to move it, and scroll to zoom.

```{r}
team <- data.frame(
  from = c("Ana", "Ana", "Ana", "Ben", "Ben", "Chloe", "Chloe", "Dev",
           "Eve", "Eve", "Farid", "Gus", "Gus", "Hana", "Hana", "Ivo",
           "Jo", "Jo", "Kim", "Ana", "Eve"),
  to = c("Ben", "Chloe", "Dev", "Chloe", "Dev", "Dev", "Eve", "Eve",
         "Farid", "Gus", "Gus", "Hana", "Ivo", "Ivo", "Jo", "Jo",
         "Kim", "Lea", "Lea", "Hana", "Kim")
)
people <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Chloe", "Dev", "Eve", "Farid", "Gus", "Hana",
           "Ivo", "Jo", "Kim", "Lea"),
  team = rep(c("Product", "Engineering", "Sales"), each = 4)
)
network_graph(team, from = "from", to = "to", nodes = people,
              node_group = "team", title = "Who works with whom")
```

By default the nodes are sized by their number of links. With `directed = TRUE`, the links become arrows:

```{r}
pairs <- as.data.frame(unique(mpg[, c("manufacturer", "class")]))
network_graph(pairs, from = "manufacturer", to = "class", directed = TRUE,
              charge = -220, title = "Which manufacturers make which classes")
```
